edges.notes: Node OS provides kernel; Linux dominates documented deployments.
Kubelet and control plane components often installed as systemd units on Linux; not universal.
Node services (kubelet, container runtime, kube-proxy, …) are commonly expressed as systemd unit files on Linux.
Ecosystem overlap: local clusters, historical CRI-dockerd patterns; production often containerd/CRI-O.
kubelet uses CRI; containerd is a common implementation (CRI-O and others also exist).
Pod workloads are commonly specified as OCI images pulled and unpacked by the node CRI stack.
Image pulls from container registries use distribution-class HTTP APIs at the registry boundary.
Linux nodes run pod containers as OCI bundles via CRI and low-level OCI runtimes.
Cluster and CI image-build pipelines use BuildKit alongside kubelet/CRI; build is not the same as pod execution.
Helm installs and upgrades Kubernetes workloads from charts via the Kubernetes API; complementary to kubelet/CRI image pulls.
Flux controllers run on Kubernetes and reconcile Git/OCI sources into cluster state via the Kubernetes API.
Argo CD runs on Kubernetes and reconciles Git-declared application state into the cluster via the Kubernetes API.
Kustomize builds Kubernetes manifests consumed by kubectl, CI, and GitOps controllers operating against the Kubernetes API.
Nodes configured with crun-backed CRI stacks run workloads through the same kubelet/CRI path.
CRI-O is a common alternative CRI implementation on Linux (especially OpenShift-class deployments).
Substitutable orchestrator class in some on-prem and edge deployments; not mutually exclusive in knowledge model.
Managed cloud orchestrator substitution for container workloads; different API and portability model.
Parallel-era cluster managers; Mesos retired — comparative framing only.
Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes-conformant clusters and installs Kubernetes APIs per AWS documentation (managed offering).
Microsoft documents AKS as a managed Kubernetes service with Azure-operated control plane (managed offering).
Google documents GKE as Kubernetes clusters with Google-managed control plane (managed offering).
Microsoft documents Azure Container Apps as powered by Kubernetes (without exposing the Kubernetes API directly).
Oracle documents OKE as CNCF-conformant Kubernetes on OCI (managed offering).
IBM documents IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service as a certified managed Kubernetes offering (managed relationship).
Microsoft documents AKS virtual nodes that run pods as Azure Container Instances container groups (Kubernetes workload backing).
DigitalOcean documents DOKS as a Kubernetes service with a fully managed control plane (managed offering relationship).
Civo documents managed Kubernetes certified conformant by CNCF (managed offering relationship).
Akamai documents LKE as a managed Kubernetes engine built on Kubernetes (managed offering relationship).
Broadcom documents Tanzu Kubernetes Grid as an opinionated open-source Kubernetes configuration with validated binaries (distribution relationship to upstream Kubernetes).
Red Hat documents OpenShift Container Platform with Kubernetes as a core component and a fully accessible Kubernetes API to the cluster (platform relationship to upstream Kubernetes).
Red Hat documents OpenShift Dedicated as offering OpenShift Container Platform clusters as a managed service on AWS or Google Cloud (managed offering relationship).
Pod workloads on Linux nodes frequently use Alpine-class OCI images; not exclusive to Alpine.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use Debian-class glibc userlands; not exclusive to Debian.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use Ubuntu-class glibc userlands; not exclusive to Ubuntu.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use Fedora-class or RHEL-family glibc userlands; not exclusive to Fedora.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use RHEL-class glibc userlands on enterprise Kubernetes footprints; not exclusive to RHEL.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use Rocky Linux-class glibc userlands; not exclusive to Rocky Linux.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use AlmaLinux-class glibc userlands; not exclusive to AlmaLinux.
Pod workloads and node OS choices frequently use CentOS Stream-class glibc userlands; not exclusive to CentOS Stream.
Pod workloads and node OS choices historically used CentOS Linux-class glibc userlands; not exclusive to CentOS Linux.
Linux nodes commonly use kube-proxy iptables/nftables modes that program netfilter unless replaced by other datapaths.
Some stacks run VM-class workloads (KVM-backed) alongside or instead of default OCI containers; distinct from kubelet’s default pod sandbox.
KubeVirt-class stacks may compose libvirt/QEMU/KVM on nodes; cite product-specific docs per claim.
KubeVirt extends Kubernetes with VM CRDs and controllers; Kubernetes remains the orchestration plane for those objects per KubeVirt documentation.
Kata Containers integrates with Kubernetes via RuntimeClass and CRI paths for VM-isolated OCI workloads per Kata documentation.
gVisor’s runsc integrates with Kubernetes via RuntimeClass and CRI paths for syscall-interposed OCI workloads per gVisor documentation.
